questions.question: In the series 2, 3, 5, 8, 12, ..., what pattern connects the terms?
options: A constant difference of 1
A constant ratio of 1.5
The differences between terms increase by 1 each time (1, 2, 3, 4)
Each term is a perfect square
questions.rationale: The differences are 1, 2, 3, 4 — increasing by 1 each step. This is a second-order (difference-of-differences) pattern rather than a simple arithmetic or geometric one.

questions.question: What should you suspect when no simple arithmetic, geometric, or difference-based rule fits a number series?
options: The question has no valid answer
An alternating series — split it into two interleaved sub-series and test each separately
The series must involve only prime numbers
The series is definitely miswritten
questions.rationale: Many series interleave two separate patterns on odd and even positions. Splitting the series into its two sub-sequences and testing each independently often reveals the hidden rule.

questions.question: In the alphabet series B, D, F, H, ?, what is the next letter?
options: I
J
K
L
questions.rationale: Positions are 2, 4, 6, 8 — increasing by 2 each time. The next position is 10, which is J.

questions.question: In the series X, Z, B, D, why doesn't the pattern break after Z?
options: It does break — Z is the wrong term
The alphabet wraps around, so after Z the sequence continues from A
This is not a valid alphabet series
Z is always the last term allowed in any series
questions.rationale: The alphabet is treated as a loop of 26 letters for series purposes, so a skip-pattern series can wrap from Z back to A and continue normally.

questions.question: In the series 3, 6, 12, 24, 48, ?, what is the next term?
questions.rationale: The ratio between consecutive terms is constant at x2 (a geometric series), so 48 x 2 = 96.

questions.question: What is the next term in 1, 8, 27, 64, ?
questions.rationale: These are cubes of consecutive integers (1^3, 2^3, 3^3, 4^3), so the next term is 5^3 = 125.

questions.question: In the alphabet series A, C, E, G, ?, what comes next?
options: H
I
J
K
questions.rationale: The series skips one letter each time (A, C, E, G); continuing the skip-pattern gives I next.

questions.question: Find the wrong term: 3, 6, 12, 24, 46, 96
questions.rationale: Testing a constant x2 ratio throughout gives 3, 6, 12, 24, 48, 96 — so 46 breaks the pattern and should be 48.

questions.question: In the alternating series 1, 10, 3, 8, 5, 6, 7, ?, what is the next term?
questions.rationale: Splitting into two sub-series: odd positions (1, 3, 5, 7) increase by 2, even positions (10, 8, 6, ?) decrease by 2, so the next even-position term is 4.

questions.question: After ruling out a constant difference and a constant ratio, what should you check next according to the solving strategy?
options: Whether the series is alphabetic
Whether the differences between terms form their own simple pattern
Whether the series is a trick question
Whether the series has an odd number of terms
questions.rationale: Step 4 of the solving strategy is to check whether the differences themselves form a pattern, which catches most second-order series that don't fit a simple arithmetic or geometric rule.
